name: Fatty liver disease (MASLD)
definition: A common condition in which fat builds up in the liver, often linked to being overweight.
overview: Fatty liver disease linked to metabolic problems is now called MASLD and was formerly known as non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD). The NHS says it can usually be treated with healthy lifestyle changes. It does not usually cause symptoms and is often found through tests done for another reason. The British Liver Trust says most cases stay mild, but in a small number of people the condition can progress to scarring, cirrhosis, liver failure or liver cancer.
causes: Fat builds up in the liver, often in people who are overweight.
Obesity, metabolic syndrome and type 2 diabetes raise the risk.
Gene variants that increase the risk have been found in research funded by NIDDK.
riskFactors: Being overweight, especially with fat around the waist
An unhealthy diet or low physical activity
High blood pressure or high cholesterol
Smoking, which NI Direct adds to the list
signs: Yellow skin and eyes (jaundice), or swelling of the ankles and abdomen, in advanced disease
complications: Inflammation of the liver (MASH, formerly NASH)
Cirrhosis, in which the liver shrinks and becomes scarred and lumpy
Liver failure and liver cancer in a small number of people
A higher chance of developing type 2 diabetes
diagnosis: The NHS says a GP asks about symptoms and alcohol intake and measures height, weight and waist. Further blood tests or an ultrasound scan may follow, to confirm fat in the liver, rule out other causes and check for liver damage. A liver biopsy is sometimes needed, mainly when the diagnosis is in doubt or cirrhosis is a concern. NICE recommends offering people with NAFLD testing for advanced liver fibrosis. It also suggests considering the enhanced liver fibrosis (ELF) test.
treatment: The NHS describes healthy lifestyle change as the main treatment. People without liver damage do not usually need specialist care, whereas those with fibrosis or cirrhosis are seen by a liver specialist. The NHS mentions pioglitazone or vitamin E as options in that setting. The British Liver Trust adds that medicines may be used for linked conditions such as type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure and high cholesterol.
prevention: The British Liver Trust gives a healthy diet, regular physical activity and a healthy weight as the first approach. The NHS also advises not smoking.
seekCare: NHS 111 Wales advises seeing a GP urgently, or calling NHS 111, for jaundice, itchy skin or swelling of the legs or abdomen in someone with a known liver condition. MedlinePlus lists persistent tiredness or pain in the upper right abdomen as reasons for assessment, and a routine GP appointment is the usual first step in the UK. Vomiting blood or collapse is an emergency, and the route is to call 999.

sections.heading: What is fatty liver disease and what are its stages?
sections.body:
Fatty liver disease means fat has built up in the liver, and the NHS says it is a common condition. The name has changed over time: it was long called non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, and the British Liver Trust now uses metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, or MASLD. Its more serious form, in which the liver is also inflamed, is now called MASH and was previously called NASH. NIDDK describes simple fatty liver and the inflamed form as two types of the same disease.

NHS hospital leaflets describe four stages: simple fatty liver, inflammation, scarring and cirrhosis. In cirrhosis the liver shrinks and becomes scarred and lumpy, and the damage is permanent. The British Liver Trust estimates that about 1 in 4 adults in the UK have MASLD. A 2023 consensus statement it cites puts the figure at up to 1 in 3.

sections.heading: Does fatty liver disease cause symptoms?
sections.body:
The NHS says fatty liver disease does not usually cause symptoms. NIDDK calls it a silent disease with few or no symptoms. It is therefore often found through blood tests or scans done for another reason. Some people feel very tired or generally unwell, according to the NHS. Others notice discomfort in the upper right side of the abdomen, under the ribs. MedlinePlus lists persistent tiredness or upper right abdominal pain among reasons for assessment.

NHS hospital leaflets note that some symptoms may come from linked conditions such as diabetes, high blood pressure, sleep apnoea or heart disease. In advanced disease, yellow skin and eyes (jaundice) or swelling of the ankles and abdomen can appear. NIDDK warns, on its page for children, that by the time symptoms arise there may already be permanent liver damage.

sections.heading: How is fatty liver disease diagnosed?
sections.body:
The NHS says a GP will ask about symptoms and about how much alcohol a person drinks. The GP also measures height, weight and waist size. Further blood tests or an ultrasound scan may follow, to confirm fat in the liver, to rule out other causes and to look for liver damage. NIDDK says doctors may use blood tests, imaging and a liver biopsy to diagnose the disease and to tell simple fatty liver from the inflamed form. A patient information sheet used in the NHS says a biopsy is sometimes needed, mainly when the diagnosis is in doubt or cirrhosis is a concern.

Fibrosis means scarring of the liver. NICE recommends that people with NAFLD are offered testing for advanced liver fibrosis. It also says the enhanced liver fibrosis (ELF) test can be considered. NICE material advises that adults and young people found to have advanced fibrosis are referred to a liver specialist.

sections.heading: How is fatty liver disease treated?
sections.body:
The NHS describes lifestyle change as the main treatment. That means a balanced diet, regular exercise and weight loss for people who are overweight. NIDDK also names weight loss as the main recommendation, because it can reduce liver fat, inflammation and scarring. The British Liver Trust cites evidence that losing 5 to 10 per cent of body weight can control the condition and in some cases reverse it. The NHS advises regular check-ups for people without liver damage, at least once a year. People without liver damage do not usually need specialist care.

When fibrosis or cirrhosis is present, a liver specialist becomes involved, and the NHS mentions pioglitazone or vitamin E as options. MedlinePlus describes resmetirom, used with diet and exercise, for adults with NASH without cirrhosis who have moderate to advanced scarring. NIDDK says certain diabetes medicines can effectively improve NASH. The British Liver Trust adds that medicines may treat linked conditions such as type 2 diabetes, high blood pressure and high cholesterol.

sections.heading: How is fatty liver disease linked to type 2 diabetes and cirrhosis?
sections.body:
The NHS lists type 2 diabetes among the risk factors for fatty liver disease. NIDDK says obesity and type 2 diabetes both raise the chance that simple fatty liver progresses to inflammation and scarring. The link runs both ways: one review reports that people with MASLD have a two to five times higher risk of developing type 2 diabetes than the general population. The same review reports that diabetes in people with MASLD is linked to a higher risk of serious liver complications and of liver cancer. In a study of repeated liver biopsies, type 2 diabetes was linked to a higher risk of scarring getting worse.

One review describes the disease as a spectrum running from simple fatty liver through inflammation to cirrhosis and liver cancer. Authors of reviews recommend finding MASLD early in people with diabetes.

sections.heading: What is the outlook, and when should a person get help?
sections.body:
The British Liver Trust says most cases stay mild. It also says a small number of people progress to serious liver disease. The trust points to weight loss as something that can, in some cases, reverse the condition. The NHS adds that, without liver damage, specialist care is not usually needed. The trust also runs a free, nurse-led helpline for people with liver conditions.

NHS 111 Wales advises seeing a GP urgently, or calling NHS 111, for jaundice, itchy skin or swelling of the legs or abdomen in someone with a known liver condition. Persistent tiredness or pain under the right ribs would normally be raised at a routine GP appointment. Vomiting blood or collapse is an emergency, and the route is to call 999.

faqs.q: Can fatty liver disease be reversed?
faqs.a: The NHS says it can usually be treated with healthy lifestyle changes. The British Liver Trust cites evidence that losing 5 to 10 per cent of body weight can control the condition and sometimes reverse it. NIDDK says weight loss can reduce liver fat, inflammation and scarring. Established cirrhosis damage is described in NHS leaflets as permanent.

faqs.q: Is MASLD the same as NAFLD?
faqs.a: MASLD is the newer name for what was called non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, or NAFLD. The inflamed form, MASH, was previously called NASH. The British Liver Trust says steatotic liver disease is now used as an umbrella term for the various causes of fat in the liver. Some older pages and leaflets still use the earlier names.

faqs.q: Does alcohol matter in fatty liver disease?
faqs.a: The NHS says a GP asks about alcohol intake when assessing the liver. One NHS hospital leaflet advises avoiding alcohol and describes MASLD as associated with being overweight or obese, or having diabetes. Blood tests or an ultrasound scan may also be used to rule out other causes of fat build-up.

faqs.q: Who is more likely to get fatty liver disease?
faqs.a: The NHS lists being overweight, an unhealthy diet or low activity, type 2 diabetes, polycystic ovary syndrome, high blood pressure or cholesterol, and being over 50. NIDDK names obesity, metabolic syndrome and type 2 diabetes as factors that raise the risk of the disease.

faqs.q: Does fatty liver disease always lead to cirrhosis?
faqs.a: No: the British Liver Trust says most cases stay mild. A small number of people progress to scarring, cirrhosis, liver failure or liver cancer. The NHS advises regular check-ups, at least once a year, for people who have no liver damage.
